title: Robotic Pack-to-Cell Teardown for E-Bike Fleets
one_liner: A robot cell driven by a vision-language-action model that opens e-bike and scooter packs, tests every cell, and regrades them for low-cost storage.
customer: Delivery-app fleet operators, e-bike and scooter share operators, battery-swap networks and repair shops (pay per pack), with buyers of graded cells for stationary storage.
problem: Micromobility packs are the high-volume end-of-life lithium stream arriving now, while EV end-of-life will not dominate until after 2040. Manual teardown is dangerous and slow, so packs go to shredders at low value or sit in shops as fire risks.
solution: A cell with a robot foundation model fine-tuned on pack disassembly with force feedback. It cuts nickel strips, pulls cells, tests each one (IR and impedance), grades A/B/C, and repackages A-grade cells for stationary storage or tools. C-grade goes to recyclers. It starts as a manual-plus-robotic service in one city.
why_now: 2025-26 robot foundation models made unstructured manipulation tasks feasible, and e-bike fire scrutiny gives fleets a reason to pay.
revenue_model: Fee per pack processed, plus margin on graded cells, plus recycler payments for C-grade.
non_obvious_insight: Recyclers built for EV packs face feed that is 15 years late. E-bike packs are small enough that a robot cell amortizes quickly, and their cells are far from dead.
first_30_days: Contract with 2 fleet operators or a swap network in NYC or LA. Rent a bench with a fire-safe enclosure and cell testers. Process 500 packs manually to build the dataset and unit economics before adding the robot.

title: Slop-Rating Feed for Kids' Filters
one_liner: A channel- and app-level data feed that classifies children's content as verified human-made, AI slop or unknown, sold to school web filters and kids' hardware.
customer: School-district web-filter and parental-control vendors, kids' tablet, audio-player and smart-speaker makers, and school districts directly.
problem: Fairplay found that 104 of the first 500 videos recommended to a fresh account were AI slop. On 1 Apr 2026 more than 200 organisations, including the American Federation of Teachers, asked YouTube to label and ban AI content on kids' surfaces, and YouTube said only that it is developing labels. Filters classify by topic (violence, adult), not by how content was produced.
solution: Continuously crawl kids-targeted channels, apps, audiobooks and games. Classify provenance using channel behaviour, voice and image-model signals, upload cadence and template reuse, plus human review. Add a 'verified human-made' tier through creator attestations and audits. Deliver category lists by API keyed on channel ID, domain or app package, plus teacher whitelist packs.
why_now: Spring 2026 investigations (NYT, Fairplay, CBC) and the April coalition letter made AI slop a school and parent issue. The EU AI Act's Article 50 labelling is beginning, and 1:1 school device fleets need a new filter category now.
revenue_model: $20-200k per year data licences to filter vendors, $0.10-0.50 per-device royalties from hardware makers, and $1-3 per student per year for districts.
non_obvious_insight: A platform's own AI label will always be optional and gameable. The buyer is whoever sits between the child and the platform, and they already buy category feeds. Selling a new dimension (provenance) into an existing distribution channel avoids consumer acquisition entirely.
first_30_days: Build a 20k-channel labelled seed set with three teacher or parent reviewers. Ship a free 'slop score' browser extension for teachers to collect signals and leads. Pitch three mid-size filter and parental-control vendors with a sample feed.

title: Rolling Bio-Uplift Trials for Frontier Labs
one_liner: A standing cohort of novices and benign-proxy wet-lab tasks that measures whether each new AI model actually helps people do biology, within weeks of release.
customer: Frontier AI lab safeguards and preparedness teams, government AI safety institutes, and operators of bio-AI verification programs; insurers later.
problem: The main large RCT (Active Site, n=153, run June-August 2025, published February 2026) found workflow completion of 5.2% with LLMs versus 6.6% with the internet. Task uplift was 1.42x and non-significant. Forecasters had predicted 27% uplift against 5% actual. By publication the tested models were about a year old. Labs now grant relaxed safeguards to verified users (Anthropic's Sept 17 program) without current evidence on which wet-lab tasks models actually change.
solution: Maintain a trained standing cohort of 100-200 novices with baselined tacit skill, in a BSL-1 lab with IRB approval done once. Use pre-approved benign-proxy tasks (plasmid construction with harmless markers, protein purification, cell culture, plaque assay with a harmless phage). Randomize model access versus internet access and return results within 2-3 weeks of each model checkpoint.
why_now: The RCT showed tacit bench skill, not knowledge, is the bottleneck, and it also exposed evaluation lag. Frontier labs ship models every few months. New verification programs make evidence on actual uplift commercially valuable to both labs and legitimate users.
revenue_model: $150-400k per model evaluation, $600k-1.5M annual retainers, and calibrated benchmark licenses to verification-program operators.
non_obvious_insight: The frontier is mostly measured with text quizzes, while risk (and benefit to legitimate labs) lives in hands-on tacit skill. Speed and cadence, not a one-off academic RCT, is the product. Active Site is a nonprofit incumbent, so expect to partner or license protocols. The cohort and lab double as a training and vetting pipeline for a bench network.
first_30_days: Contact Active Site and METR alumni for protocol and IRB templates and explore licensing rather than duplicating. Secure BSL-1 space. Recruit 40 novices and run a 3-week pilot on two open-weight models to publish methodology. Pitch 3 safeguards teams and 2 government safety bodies on a $100k pilot.

title: Community Radio as a Paid Knowledge API
one_liner: Turn African community-radio call-in shows into a live, district-level, per-call-priced local-truth feed that farm agents and lenders pay for, with stations keeping most of the revenue.
customer: Agri-input distributors, crop insurers, agri-lenders and farmer-facing AI agents (FarmerChat-style services) in East Africa. Community radio stations in Uganda and Kenya are the supply side and get 70% of revenue.
problem: Western models 'fail spectacularly' on African crops, and satellites cannot see this week's pest outbreak, local planting window or market price. Community radio is where farmers self-report and where trusted extension voices answer, but its ad revenue is collapsing. Bots do not click ads, so stations earn nothing when agents consume their knowledge.
solution: Transcribe and structure weekly call-in shows (Luganda, Swahili, Hausa and others) into dated, sourced, district-level signals such as pest reports, price quotes and planting advice, with provenance and consent. Expose them as an MCP or HTTP endpoint with per-call micropayments via x402 or MPP. Add a paid 'ask the station' tier where an agent's question is read on air and the answer captured. Stations receive rev-share via mobile money.
why_now: Small ASR models (300M-1.7B parameters) now handle local languages, and AethexAI already trains on radio audio. FarmerChat has answered 8M+ questions, which proves demand. Machine-payment protocols make micro-charging per call possible, and Cloudflare's pay-per-crawl is training content owners to charge bots.
revenue_model: Per-call fees for agents ($0.005-0.05), district-level monthly subscriptions ($200-600) for lenders and insurers, and premium on-air Q&A. Platform keeps 30% and stations get 70%.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a language training set, which is a commodity. It is fresh local ground truth with a trusted human voice behind it, delivered as a live feed rather than an archive. Radio stations are the last network where farmers report in their own words. Content owners who cannot win the ad economy can win the agent-query economy.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 stations in Uganda and Kenya with a simple rev-share and consent agreement. Record and transcribe two weeks of shows with a fine-tuned open ASR model. Publish a weekly district JSON feed. Sell the first two district subscriptions to an agri-lender or seed distributor at $300-500 a month.

title: Appeal Kits for Musicians Wrongly Flagged as AI
one_liner: A DAW-side watcher that quietly notarizes your project history, so a wrongful 'AI' flag becomes a one-click appeal instead of a lost royalty stream.
customer: Independent producers and singer-songwriters releasing 5-50 tracks a year on TIDAL, Deezer, Spotify and Bandcamp, plus small labels and distributor support desks that have to rule on flagged tracks.
problem: Platforms now punish fully-AI tracks: TIDAL demonetizes them (Jul 15, 2026), Spotify excludes AI-persona profiles from recommendations (Aug 11), and Bandcamp banned AI music outright (Jan 14). Detectors are probabilistic, and with AI above 50% of Deezer uploads, thresholds will tighten and false positives will grow (my inference). A wrongly flagged human has no evidence and no appeal format. The free verified-artist badges do nothing for someone already flagged.
solution: A background agent for Ableton, Logic, Reaper and FL Studio (Ableton .als files are gzipped XML, so they diff cleanly) that hashes project files, stems, plugin chains and automation over time. It anchors the hashes to a public timestamp log and renders a shareable 'Session Timeline' page. One click exports an appeal packet formatted for each platform's dispute flow, with a verify link that distributors can check. Artists choose what to reveal and never upload raw sessions.
why_now: Enforcement went live in a six-month burst (Bandcamp Jan 2026, TIDAL Jul 15, Spotify Aug 11), so 'flagged as AI' now costs money and reach rather than a label. Detection is increasingly automated and at volume. Nobody has built the defendant's side of the process.
revenue_model: $9/month artist plan, $49 per notarized appeal packet for non-subscribers, $500-2,000/month label plans, and a per-verification API fee from distributors that want to clear flagged-track disputes faster.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody pays for proof-of-human in advance, because the badge is free. They pay at the moment of dispute. Sell the evidence, like a dashcam that is only valued after the crash, and not the badge.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: build a project-file watcher for Ableton and Reaper with a hosted timeline page. Weeks 3-4: recruit 30 producers from r/WeAreTheMusicMakers and producer Discords, and DM artists who have posted about false AI flags. Offer a free install and charge only for the first appeal packet. Pitch two distributor support leads on accepting the verify link.

title: Rights-Request Engine for Rejected Applicants
one_liner: A consumer tool that files legally formatted data-access and automated-decision requests to employers' hiring systems, turning silent rejections into scores, reasons and evidence.
customer: Job seekers, starting in the UK and EU under GDPR Art. 15/22, then Illinois and California. They pay $12 a month or $29 per request pack. Secondary buyers are plaintiff-side employment firms and researchers who license opt-in aggregate data.
problem: Applicants send dozens of applications, get almost no replies and never learn why (HN: 65 applications, 3 phone screens, 0 interviews). New laws give people rights to see and contest automated screening, but nobody uses them because finding the right contact and format is a hassle.
solution: A browser extension logs each application (company, ATS vendor, date). After 30 days of silence it files a data-access and automated-decision request, tracks the one-month deadline, escalates to the regulator, and parses the response into a structured 'why I was screened out' report. Opt-in aggregate stats show which employers and ATS vendors auto-reject which profiles.
why_now: California's automated-decision regulations start binding in Jan 2027 and Illinois' AI-in-employment notice law took effect Jan 2026. The Mobley v. Workday collective action is live and AI resume screening is ubiquitous. Job-search desperation is at a peak, and EU/UK rights already work today.
revenue_model: Consumer subscription or per-pack fees, plus opt-in anonymised data and insight licences to labor economists, unions and employment plaintiff firms. Employer-side compliance-readiness upsell later.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators created rights but no practical channel, and that friction is the enforcement gap. The service converts individual rights into aggregate leverage: an employer receiving 500 requests per role starts giving candidates real feedback, and the request-and-response dataset becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Build a GDPR-only MVP (templates, deadline tracker) for UK/EU applicants in two weeks, with a UK data-protection solicitor reviewing the templates. Seed it in UK and EU job-search communities and HN at £9 per pack. Measure response rates and refine.

title: Defense Magnet and Tungsten Provenance Dossiers
one_liner: A shared investigator that produces audit-ready provenance files on magnets and tungsten parts for the sub-tier suppliers who cannot get answers from their distributors.
customer: Small and mid-size defense sub-tier suppliers (motors, actuators, sensors, drones, speakers) that buy NdFeB, SmCo magnets or tungsten parts through distributors.
problem: DFARS magnet and tungsten sourcing restrictions extend to upstream mining and refining stages from January 2027. Small suppliers cannot compel Chinese-linked distributors or sinterers to disclose provenance, and primes will demand attestations.
solution: A dossier per part family: supplier questionnaires, document and mill-cert review, distributor-to-sinterer trace-back, and optional lab fingerprinting (trace-element and isotopic) via partner labs. It includes an attestation vault ready for prime audits and an approved-source list of non-covered and recycled suppliers.
why_now: The January 2027 DFARS deadline is about three months away as of late September 2026. Government equity deals (MP, Lithium Americas) and the BIS scrap rule show that provenance is now a national-security control.
revenue_model: $4-15K per part family, $1-3K monthly subscription for upkeep and alerts, and lab-test pass-through with margin.
non_obvious_insight: This is a paperwork problem too small for any customer to solve alone. A shared investigator with a growing fingerprint library amortizes the cost across dozens of clients and gets cheaper as it scales.
first_30_days: Build a free 'does this part need proof?' checker. Pull sub-tier contractors from public procurement records and reach out to 100 firms with the January deadline. Line up a partner lab for fingerprinting. Close 5 paid dossiers.

title: Pickleball Noise Measurement Standard and Monitoring
one_liner: A court-defensible protocol, sensor kit and certification for measuring pickleball noise, sold to towns, HOAs and clubs.
customer: Parks and planning departments, HOAs, private clubs, court builders and municipal attorneys.
problem: Paddle impacts read roughly 70-80 dBA at 15 ft against 40-55 dBA ambient, and disputes are closing or limiting courts. In April 2026 a Missouri judge voided Kirkwood's restrictions as 'arbitrary, capricious and invalid' because noise could not be consistently measured. That leaves cities, clubs and neighbors all without an enforceable standard.
solution: A measurement protocol for impulsive, tonal sports noise (peak and Leq metrics, distance and background correction), a calibrated ~$500 sensor kit with cloud reporting and automatic compliance reports, expert-witness-ready PDFs, and an 'approved low-impact site' certification that helps at permit hearings. Add mitigation advice (barriers, quiet paddles and balls).
why_now: The Kirkwood ruling and hundreds of local ordinance fights, with participation at 24.3M and rising.
revenue_model: Kit sale or rental ($500 plus $30/month monitoring), $2-5k per-site certification, $1.5k expert reports, and protocol licensing to municipalities.
non_obvious_insight: Noise fights are fights over measurement. Whoever supplies the trusted protocol becomes the referee both sides must use, and courts have already said unmeasurable ordinances fail.
first_30_days: Contact 10 town attorneys and HOA boards currently in noise disputes and offer loaner sensor rigs. Publish an open draft protocol with an acoustical-engineer advisor. Aim for the first paid report in month one.

title: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Eligibility and Prior-Auth Navigator
one_liner: A 2-minute eligibility check and clinician-ready prior-auth packet for the $50/month Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, sold to caregivers, independent pharmacies and primary-care offices before the window closes in December 2027.
customer: Two payers. (a) Gen X adult children (45-58, household income often above $100K) who manage a Medicare-age parent's medications and pay $29 per packet. (b) Independent pharmacies and small primary-care practices that pay $79/month to stop fielding the same eligibility and prior-auth questions by phone.
problem: Medicare started an 18-month GLP-1 Bridge on July 1, 2026. It costs $50/month for Wegovy, Zepbound or Foundayo, but eligibility is a maze. It needs a BMI of 35 or more, or BMI 30+ with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, uncontrolled hypertension or stage 3a+ kidney disease, or BMI 27+ with pre-diabetes, prior heart attack or stroke, or symptomatic peripheral artery disease. Type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea and MASH disqualify you. So does having filled any GLP-1 under Part D in 2026. Prior authorization is required. Roughly 3.8M Part D enrollees qualify and about 5.9M are locked out, so sicker patients are routed to Part D copays of $200-600+ a month. One 68-year-old retired professor with BMI 42, a quadruple bypass and sleep apnea told KFF Health News: 'I'm obese, morbidly obese, BMI 42... And yet I can't get it.'
solution: A plain-language quiz built from the published Bridge criteria. It flags the traps, such as a 2026 Part D GLP-1 fill or a sleep apnea diagnosis. It outputs one of three routes: Bridge, Part D with an expected copay, or a manufacturer cash price (TrumpRx lists $149-$299/month). It then generates a prior-authorization documentation checklist and cover letter for the prescriber (BMI evidence, comorbidity codes, exclusion attestation). Pharmacies and practices get a white-label link and a shared queue of who is waiting on what. It stays plan-neutral: no plan enrollment and no commissions from carriers, which keeps it outside Medicare marketing rules (confirm with counsel).
why_now: The Bridge began July 1, 2026 and ends December 2027, so the demand window is 15 months and open enrollment starts October 15, about 3 weeks from now. CMS is also ending the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026. That subsidy had cut average premiums by $26 in 2025 and $16 in 2026, and about 24.9M people are in stand-alone drug plans that may face bigger 2027 increases. Oral options (Wegovy pill approved December 2025, Foundayo approved April 2026) widen the eligible pool. Nobody has built a workflow product for a program this new and this temporary.
revenue_model: $29 one-time per beneficiary packet (caregiver-paid). $79/month per independent pharmacy or clinic for white-label link, queue and templates. Optional $15 per completed PA-submission assist. Sunset risk is real, so design the engine to carry over to whatever CMS replaces the Bridge with (KFF flags a coming BALANCE model).
non_obvious_insight: The eligibility rules create a paradox where the sicker you are, the more you pay. Sleep apnea or diabetes disqualifies patients from the $50 Bridge and pushes them into $200-600+ Part D copays, which can exceed manufacturer cash prices ($199 Wegovy pen, $299 Zepbound on TrumpRx). That gap creates demand for a neutral router rather than another telehealth prescriber. Evidence: KFF's Bridge criteria, cost and start/end dates https://www.kff.org/medicare/nearly-four-million-medicare-beneficiaries-met-the-eligibility-criteria-in-2023-for-the-medicare-glp-1-bridge/ ; the excluded-patient quote, 5.9M figure and Part D copay range https://kffhealthnews.org/aging/medicare-glp1-bridge-weight-loss-drugs-coverage-exceptions-cost-access/ ; premium-subsidy end and 24.9M stand-alone enrollees https://www.kff.org/quick-insights/cmss-decision-to-end-temporary-subsidies-to-medicares-stand-alone-drug-plans-could-mean-larger-premium-increases-for-some-beneficiaries-next-year/ ; cash prices https://trumprx.gov/ . To verify: whether Medicare beneficiaries can actually use cash-price channels, and how those purchases interact with Part D cap accounting. One fetched source (Wikipedia) implies TrumpRx has Medicare-specific pricing, which conflicts with the site's consumer prices.
first_30_days: Week 1: turn the KFF criteria into a quiz and publish 'Do I qualify for the $50 Medicare GLP-1 Bridge?' pages timed to the October 15 open-enrollment spike. Week 2: post in Medicare and caregiver communities and pitch 10 independent pharmacies (NCPA-style networks) on a free white-label link. Week 3: get one primary-care practice to review the PA cover-letter template for clinical accuracy. Week 4: charge $29 for the packet. Target 100 paid packets and 5 pharmacies on $79/month. Keep it free of plan recommendations until compliance is reviewed.

title: Exchange for Shelved Academic Projects and Null Data
one_liner: Buy the 'graveyard' of academic labs, meaning abandoned projects, validated knockout lines, half-built assays and failed-experiment data, and resell them as dossiers with an interview slot to seed biotechs and AI-bio data teams. Supply is anchored by a paid lab-closure clearance service.
customer: Sellers: departing postdocs, PIs downsizing or closing labs, and department chairs and EHS offices who must clear the space. Buyers: seed biotech founders, AI-bio and virtual-cell model companies that need experimental data including null results, pharma target-validation groups, and CROs that need validated cell models. Dossiers sell for $3-30k, and closure concierge fees run $5-15k.
problem: Every lab has a graveyard: KO lines, reporter constructs, a half-optimized assay, a screen that didn't pan out, and boxes in the -80 labeled 'JK 3/14 P3 #2'. When a postdoc leaves or a lab shrinks, the physical items are discarded or become orphaned, and the reasons the project failed leave in the postdoc's head. Meanwhile a startup or AI-bio team pays 12 months and $500k to rebuild the same tools and rediscover the same dead ends. Published literature is heavily biased toward positives, and models trained only on positives are systematically overconfident.
solution: Two-sided wedge. Supply side: 'Lab Closure Concierge' is a fixed-fee triage service for labs that are closing or downsizing. It inventories freezers, plasmids, cell lines and mouse lines, interviews the departing postdoc for 90 minutes to capture provenance and failure reasons (transcribed and structured with AI), disposes of hazardous items compliantly, and flags what is worth keeping. Demand side: a curated catalog of 'dossiers': the physical or digital assets, protocols, raw data including nulls, plus a paid call with the person who built them. Use a standard institutional license or MTA template with a revenue share to the university, so overloaded tech-transfer offices approve it because the alternative is a dumpster.
why_now: NIH grant terminations, indirect-cost fights and uncertain 2026 budgets are pushing labs to shrink or close. Biotech shutdowns have also left surplus bench assets (verify current scale). AI-bio companies are openly short of high-quality experimental data, especially negative data, and pay for it. Tech-transfer offices are understaffed. LLM transcription and structuring turns a 90-minute interview into a searchable dossier cheaply.
revenue_model: Closure-concierge flat fee paid by the department or PI. A 25-30% commission on dossier sales, with revenue share to seller and institution. Annual data-subscription tier for AI-bio buyers (curated null-result feeds).
non_obvious_insight: The vials are worth very little. The value is provenance plus the 'why it failed' story stored in one person's memory, and it evaporates the day the postdoc's visa or contract ends. So the product is not a marketplace for samples, it is structured exit-knowledge capture with a physical-asset appendix. Because the university owns the IP anyway, the clean structure is to make the institution a paid party rather than an obstacle.
first_30_days: Use your own postdoc network to line up 3-5 labs that are shrinking or have departing postdocs. Offer a free triage-and-catalog audit in exchange for permission to list a few assets. Produce 10 dossiers with structured interviews. Cold-email 30 seed biotechs and AI-bio data leads with the top 5 dossiers. Close one sale at $3-8k. Use that transaction to test the university revenue-share template with one tech-transfer office.

title: AI-Native Estate Settlement Firm Under Arizona ABS
one_liner: A licensed alternative business structure that runs uncontested probate and small-estate work end-to-end at a flat fee, with attorneys supervising agent-driven workflows.
customer: Families of decedents in Arizona with $100K-$2M estates (uncontested probates, small-estate affidavits, simple trust administration), referred by funeral homes, hospices, senior living communities and advisors.
problem: Hourly or percentage probate fees don't work for $300K estates, so many attorneys decline them. Families face 9-18 months (unverified estimate) and $5-20K bills, run by an overwhelmed executor.
solution: An Arizona ABS-licensed law firm using agent workflows for documents, court filings, creditor notices, asset inventory, accountings and distributions, with attorney supervision at ratios far above traditional practice. Fixed price ($2,900-$6,500) with a timeline guarantee, payable from the estate at closing, and one point of contact. Add-ons include real estate sale and tax return preparation.
why_now: Arizona has permitted non-lawyer ownership of law firms since 2021 and Utah runs a sandbox. LLMs are now reliable enough for supervised legal drafting, and Arizona has a large retiree population. The brief's estimate of $5T of yearly transfers is heavily weighted to the very wealthy, leaving middle-class estates unserved.
revenue_model: Flat fees plus ancillary margin on property sales, tax preparation and accounting.
non_obvious_insight: Hourly legal billing can't profitably serve middle-class estates, but a licensed software-first structure can undercut on price while earning better margins. The regulatory sandbox is both wedge and moat.
first_30_days: Apply for the ABS license or white-label under an existing ABS. Sign 3 funeral homes or senior communities for referrals. Run the first cases with a supervising attorney, and get counsel to review unauthorized-practice and fee-sharing rules.

title: Dog Walkers as Repeat-Pass Sidewalk Inspectors
one_liner: Pay dog walkers a few dollars a day to mount a phone on their chest and sell the resulting block-by-block sidewalk condition layer to cities, utilities, and delivery-robot operators.
customer: City public works and ADA coordinators (mid-size cities of 100k to 500k people first), plus fiber and utility contractors and sidewalk delivery-robot operators as second buyers. Walkers are the paid supply side.
problem: Cities are legally on the hook to inventory sidewalks and curb ramps and fix trip hazards. Today that means an expensive contractor van or LiDAR survey every 5 to 10 years, or 311 complaints that skew toward loud, wealthy neighborhoods. Residential side streets go stale, and nobody sees a slab heave, a missing curb ramp, or a new obstruction until someone sues or gets hurt.
solution: A harness or chest mount plus a background app that runs during walks. It records geotagged video, and an on-device model flags heaved slabs, missing or noncompliant curb ramps, obstructions, standing water, and broken glass. Faces and plates are blurred on the phone and nothing is recorded near windows or interiors. Walkers earn per validated mile (roughly $1 a mile, so about $8 to $15 a day for something they already do). The city gets a rolling map with change detection, exported to its existing GIS or asset-management tools. A free 'dog hazard' layer (glass, bait or poison reports, hot pavement, off-leash aggressive dogs) gives walkers and owners a reason to adopt it. I have not verified current competitors or municipal pricing, so both should be checked before the pitch.
why_now: In 2026 a phone can run a decent defect-detection model offline, which was not practical a few years ago. Cities face ongoing ADA sidewalk obligations and litigation risk with tight budgets, which favors cheap continuous data over big one-off surveys. Driver-sourced street imagery (Hivemapper and Nexar style) has proven that crowds get paid for mapping, but the pedestrian tier is essentially unclaimed.
revenue_model: Annual municipal data subscription, or per-mile survey pricing that undercuts contractor quotes, at roughly $20k to $150k a year per city. Secondary sales of the same data to utilities, telecom build QA, and robot-delivery mapping. Walkers are paid about 30 to 40 percent of revenue as per-mile payouts.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody walks a residential sidewalk more than a dog walker: the same 3 to 5 miles, five days a week, at a slow pace, with eyes on the ground because dogs eat everything. The scarce asset in infrastructure data is not coverage, it is repeat passes, which is what makes change detection possible. That is exactly what a walker's fixed route produces for free.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 to 20 walkers through local pet-sitter Facebook groups and Nextdoor, since they are already clustered by neighborhood. Build the capture app with a cheap phone mount and an open sidewalk-defect model fine-tuned on public sidewalk datasets. Map about 200 miles of one neighborhood, then take a before-and-after sample to a city ADA or transportation coordinator. Offer a free neighborhood pilot with a cost comparison against contractor rates, and aim for a small pilot purchase order under the city's simple-purchase threshold.

title: Alcohol Bridge: GLP-1 Addiction Care for Hospitals
one_liner: A hospital-embedded service that starts naltrexone plus semaglutide at discharge for alcohol use disorder with PEth monitoring.
customer: Hospital addiction-consult teams and liver clinics, plus health plans and employers paying for alcohol-related admissions.
problem: Only ~2% of people with alcohol use disorder get medication. A Lancet RCT (May 2026, n=108) showed semaglutide cut heavy drinking days in AUD with obesity, with NNT ~4.3 vs 7+ for approved drugs, and NIH-reported work shows added benefit on top of CBT. Phase 3 trials and the VA's CRAVE trial are running, but clinicians have no protocol, and opioid bridge clinics got settlement money while alcohol, the bigger killer, got none.
solution: A bridge service at discharge: naltrexone alone or with semaglutide (per trial eligibility, BMI 30 or more), PEth blood monitoring every 4 weeks, telehealth follow-ups and a cash-pay pill pathway, with outcome reporting on readmissions and PEth negatives.
why_now: The first RCT and NIH coverage landed in 2026, GLP-1s are now cheap and familiar, and hospitals are under margin pressure from readmissions. Off-label use requires careful protocols, so first movers will set the standard.
revenue_model: $250-400 per patient per month billed to hospitals, payers or employers, plus grant and state SUD funds where eligible.
non_obvious_insight: Alcohol-related admissions repeat and cost the hospital, but no service line owns the medication step. The wedge is a discharge protocol, not a new clinic.
first_30_days: Approach 3 hospital addiction-consult teams and hepatology clinics. Recruit an addiction-boarded medical director and run a 30-patient quality-improvement pilot under the hospital's existing governance, charging a ~$20k pilot fee.

title: Remote Operator-of-Record for Small Water Systems
one_liner: A roll-up of certified operator licenses and contracts, with cheap remote telemetry so one operator can be operator-of-record for 10-30 small systems.
customer: Small towns, rural water districts, mobile-home and RV parks, HOAs and private systems in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Oklahoma and Iowa. The system pays a monthly fee, and state technical-assistance funds can help.
problem: State law requires a certified operator in responsible charge, yet operators are retiring and small systems cannot hire. Missed sampling and reporting cause violations. The 2027 PFAS initial monitoring and the LCRI lead changes (action level tightens Nov 1, 2027) add workload that these systems cannot absorb.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired operators as a paid bench. Install cellular SCADA gateways ($1-3k hardware) and a compliance calendar (sampling, consumer confidence reports, PFAS and lead tasks). Add on-call field technicians. Start with states that allow remote responsible charge, and with private systems where the sales cycle is shortest.
why_now: The retirement wave, the 2027 monitoring and lead deadlines, $7.2B in FY2026 revolving-fund money (some for small-system assistance), and cheap remote telemetry all coincide.
revenue_model: $3-12k/month per system, plus a compliance-concierge upsell for PFAS and lead sampling packages.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation requires a licensed human, not a plant, so the scarce asset is license-hours. Remote monitoring multiplies each license roughly tenfold. The roll-up is of licenses and contracts, not of plants.
first_30_days: Recruit three retired Grade 2-4 operators. Sign five private systems (mobile-home park owners first). Partner with a state rural water association for referrals. Confirm your state's rules on remote responsible charge with the regulator before selling.

title: Care-Home Trigger Desk: Evacuate, Shelter, Cool
one_liner: Automatic, pre-contracted action triggers that move older residents before fire, flood or heat-driven power loss becomes lethal.
customer: Multi-site senior living, assisted living and nursing operators in wildfire, coastal and heat-prone states, and their liability insurers.
problem: Older adults dominate heat, fire and hurricane deaths. Federal emergency-preparedness rules require plans but not pre-committed execution: buses, generator fuel, receiving-facility agreements and staff call-ins. Loss of power in heat kills.
solution: A facility-specific trigger sheet tied to near-real-time satellite fire detection, fire-spread modeling, AI weather ensembles and grid outage alerts. It launches staged actions: pre-contracted transport with SLAs, receiving-facility agreements, generator fuel top-ups and cooling-room setup, with an audit trail and drill simulations. Sold per bed per month.
why_now: Near-real-time satellite fire detection is getting funded and commercial (Satellites on Fire raised $2.7M), AI forecasting is cheap, and the summer 2026 heat set off demand for concrete heat plans.
revenue_model: $8-20 per bed per month, transport contract margin and insurer premium credits.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not information but pre-committed execution. Care homes have a legal duty and insurer pressure to buy it.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 operators in California and Colorado, build trigger sheets for 20 facilities, and sign transport partners.

title: Supply-Continuity Escrow for Hardware Startups
one_liner: Software-style source-code escrow, but for physical products: startups deposit CAD, BOMs and tooling data, and a pre-qualified micro-factory network is contractually obligated to keep making parts for buyers if the startup dies.
customer: Hardware startups selling to risk-averse institutional buyers (hospitals, cities, universities, fleet operators, utilities) who pay the fee, plus the buyers themselves as beneficiaries of an activation right.
problem: Procurement teams fear vendor death more than defects. A city buying 200 startup e-scooters or chargers, or a hospital buying a startup's carts or robots, has no continuity plan, so deals stall or die. When a hardware company collapses, its fleet is orphaned. The roughly 11,000 Fisker Ocean owners spent two years building their own parts supply chain through a nonprofit.
solution: A continuity package. Startups deposit CAD, drawings, BOM, supplier list, firmware build environment and key tooling data. We validate it by making trial 'trigger-ready' proof parts on printers, CNC and short-run PCB partners so that the plan is real and tested. A contract gives named buyers release rights on defined triggers (bankruptcy, 90 days with no shipments, end-of-life). Result: a one-page Continuity Letter the startup attaches to bids.
why_now: Hardware failures have piled up (Fisker, Canoo, Nikola and other consumer and mobility failures), so procurement officers have fresh horror stories. Low-cost printing, CNC and small-batch PCB fabrication now make it plausible to reproduce a wide range of parts locally without the original supply chain. Cities and health systems are buying more startup hardware in robotics, mobility and charging.
revenue_model: Annual escrow and validation fee from the vendor ($5k to $25k based on complexity), a paid proof-of-manufacturability audit, an activation fee (10% to 20% of fabricated-parts value) when triggered, and optional buyer-side monitoring of vendor health.
non_obvious_insight: It sells like insurance with a tiny loss ratio. The physical network is only activated a few percent of the time, but the deposit and the tested proof are what unlock enterprise deals for the startup. Because the startup pays to close a sale, the network is funded by growth spend rather than by rare disaster events. The hard part is proving manufacturability in advance, and that proof is the moat.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 hardware founders who are stuck in enterprise procurement and to 3 procurement or biomed managers who have been burned before. Offer a fixed-price $2,500 Continuity Letter (checklist audit plus one proof part) to the first five. Draft a simple template agreement with a startup-friendly law firm and line up two machine shops and a PCB house as network partners.

title: Delivery Robots for Gated Communities
one_liner: Buy the sidewalk-robot fleets that failed on public streets at a discount and run them inside senior-living, campus and large apartment communities as a subscription amenity.
customer: Operators of senior-living and continuing-care communities, hospital campuses, student housing, military bases and large HOAs. They pay a monthly amenity fee.
problem: Sidewalk delivery fails on demand density, not on technology. Serve built about 2,000 robots but booked $2.65M of 2025 revenue, roughly $1.3k per robot by my arithmetic. Meanwhile private communities are labor-squeezed and struggle to get meals, pharmacy items and packages to residents.
solution: Closed-loop robots on private paths deliver dining-hall meals, pharmacy pickups, mail and supplies within one campus. Use secondhand hardware, a light fleet-management layer, and teleop backup for edge cases. Price as a fixed monthly amenity fee plus a small per-delivery charge.
why_now: Sidewalk-delivery unit economics visibly broke in 2025-26, so hardware is cheap and experienced operators are available. Vision-language navigation cuts per-site mapping cost, and last-mile contractors are closing (4XH and Ardor), which shows how expensive human delivery labor has become.
revenue_model: $3-8k a month per community platform fee, plus $1-2 per delivery. Hardware is bundled or financed. Target 8-12 robots per community at about 60% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: A subscription amenity decouples revenue from order volume, which is exactly what killed the public-street model. A private campus also removes the permit, ADA and pedestrian-liability problems and guarantees density.
first_30_days: Pick 3 continuing-care or student-housing campuses in one metro. Buy or lease 3-5 used robots from a fleet operator raising cash. Run a teleop-assisted pilot delivering meals to about 20 residents, and convert one campus to a signed LOI at about $4k a month.

title: Ear-Coach for Early-Ed Teachers, Paid by QRIS
one_liner: Classroom-audio analysis that scores teacher-child interactions the way trained CLASS observers do and coaches staff weekly, sold to centers as a path to higher state quality-rating tiers and higher reimbursement.
customer: Directors and owners of centers and small chains (5-50 sites) in states with tiered-reimbursement QRIS programs. Also QRIS coaching contractors and Head Start grantees.
problem: Insiders picture AI in early education as child-facing. The real bottleneck is the adult: the average worker earns $33,140, turnover is high and coaching is sporadic. Quality-rating tiers drive subsidy-rate bonuses, but observation-based scoring needs scarce, costly trained observers, so centers stay stuck at low stars.
solution: Opt-in classroom audio pods or teacher-worn mics with on-device diarization and transcription (no child audio retained). They score serve-and-return turns, open-ended questions, language richness and tone. Each teacher gets a 3-minute weekly micro-coaching note on their phone, and directors get a mock-CLASS 'star readiness' report before official visits.
why_now: On-device diarization and transcription are cheap and good enough. New tax credits and subsidy money (45F at 40-50%, DCFSA to $7,500) are landing in centers in 2026. Child-facing AI is drawing lawsuits, while teacher-facing AI avoids that liability.
revenue_model: $40-80 per classroom per month, plus an optional success fee (a share of the reimbursement uplift) when the center's tier rises.
non_obvious_insight: Quality is a lever on price, since higher-tier centers earn higher reimbursement, so coaching can be sold as revenue rather than a cost. Putting AI in the adult's ear sidesteps the child-AI liability wave entirely.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 centers in a state that pays tier bonuses. Record consented lessons on phones and run open-source diarization. Have two ex-CLASS observers score 20 clips to validate the model's ratings. Sell a $500 'star readiness audit' per center, then convert to a monthly plan.

title: GLP-1 Alcohol Protocols Inside Sober-Living Homes
one_liner: A turnkey semaglutide-for-alcohol-use-disorder protocol delivered through recovery residences, which supply the daily accountability, testing and peer community that telehealth prescribing lacks.
customer: Sober-living and recovery-residence operators and intensive-outpatient centers, who pass the cost into resident fees of $600-2,500 a month that are usually paid by families.
problem: Very few people with alcohol use disorder get any medication, and a Lancet RCT (May 2026, n=108) showed semaglutide cut heavy drinking days with an NNT of 4.3 versus 7+ for approved drugs. GLP-1 prescribing for it is off-label and sold as DTC telehealth to isolated individuals. Recovery houses have residents, house managers and drug testing, but no medical capability. Operators bleed occupancy and reputation on relapse evictions, and GLP-1 use in liver-compromised drinkers carries real malnutrition, muscle-loss and GI risks that need monitoring.
solution: A partner addiction-medicine physician or telehealth prescriber panel screens and consents residents, using contraindication checks and baseline labs. House managers get training and a daily check-in script (dose day, intake, nausea, cravings). A dietitian sets minimum protein and calorie floors. Weekly peer-recovery groups link medication, craving and community, with a tapering and aftercare plan at discharge. The house sees 30/60/90-day retention and abstinence data.
why_now: The 2026 Lancet RCT and $149-299 cash prices for branded GLP-1s make the drug affordable. Compounded supply is closing, which pushes demand toward branded, clinician-supervised use. Many states are certifying recovery residences, and Medicaid cuts in 2027 make private-pay operators look for outcomes-based differentiation.
revenue_model: $120-200 per resident per month from operators (passed through in rent), plus clinician-visit billing or revenue share with the prescriber, and an aftercare subscription for graduates.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for alcohol-use-disorder pharmacotherapy is adherence and monitoring, not the prescription. Telehealth sells scripts to lonely individuals, while sober-living houses already have people living together with daily check-ins and testing. The house is the missing delivery infrastructure, and GLP-1 gives it the first credible craving-reduction drug to offer.
first_30_days: Sign one addiction-medicine physician and three operators in one metro (Florida, Texas or California). Enroll about 20 consenting residents with written informed consent, and track 30/60/90-day retention and abstinence days versus the houses' baselines. Use the data to sign the next 10 houses. Get a healthcare attorney's review of the off-label and consent framework before the first dose.

title: Error-Rate Cliff Insurance for SNAP Agencies
one_liner: A managed QC service that re-reads a sample of newly approved and recertified SNAP cases against federal review rules and builds federal-dispute packets, sold to county and state agencies facing cost-share penalties.
customer: County social-services directors in county-administered states (NC, CO, MN, NY, OH, VA and others), state QC units, and state agencies with error rates at or above 6%. In FY2025, 20 states were at 10% or higher.
problem: Illinois's FY2025 SNAP error rate was 14.7%. Its DHS estimates roughly $700M of penalty exposure, is hiring 450 staff for $55M, and faces admin costs rising from $60M to $100M as the state share of SNAP admin costs goes from 50% to 75% in October 2026. In North Carolina, Wilson County's DSS (about $13M budget) faces up to $4.2M in penalties with no state relief, and the state's eligibility system (NC FAST) has no document portal or AI. Counties report ~10% vacancy and staff with about a year of experience. Illinois DHS says most errors are 'minor errors', and the federal definition of an error is any variance of $57 or more.
solution: Each week, supervisors upload a 5-10% sample of case files per caseworker. AI extracts income, household composition, deductions and verification documents, recomputes the benefit under federal and state policy, and flags variances of $57 or more with the policy citation. Supervisors get a fix-before-QC list. For cases in the federal QC sample, the tool builds the dispute or arbitration packet comparing the state review with the federal findings. Certified ex-state QC reviewers sign off on anything high-stakes. Deploy inside the county's own cloud tenant so no PII leaves.
why_now: H.R. 1 shifts benefit-cost sharing to states by error-rate tier, with the top tier at 15% of benefit costs for rates of 10% or more. Penalties begin in FY2028-29, starting October 2027 per Capitol News Illinois. The admin-cost shift hits October 2026. Agencies are also absorbing Medicaid work-requirement workloads, so they cannot hire their way to accuracy.
revenue_model: Per-case-reviewed fee ($15-40 range to test) or annual county subscription of $40-150k. For comparison, one county eligibility worker costs $40-95k a year. Optional shared-savings pricing tied to avoided penalty tier.
non_obvious_insight: The penalty is a cliff function by error-rate band, so fixing a handful of cases near a threshold can be worth millions, which makes a cheap second-look service priced like insurance. In county-administered states, each of ~100 counties (NC) is a separate small buyer that carries its own penalty exposure. The cost of the problem is in the evidence: Illinois's 14.7% rate, ~$700M exposure, 450 hires and $55M budget (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/illinois-food-assistance-error-rate-continues-to-grow-as-federal-penalties-loom/). NC's 10% vacancy, Wilson County's $4.2M penalty exposure on a $13M budget, and staff with 11-13 months' experience (https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/04/30/medicaid-work-county-challenges/). Job-posting signal: governmentjobs.com showed about 2,000 'eligibility worker' results on 2026-09-28 at roughly $40-95k salaries (https://www.governmentjobs.com/jobs?keyword=eligibility%20worker). Indiana is hiring 400 people to check eligibility (https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2026/04/29/fssa-hiring-400-medicaid-eligibility-checkers-ahead-of-work-requirements/) and Pennsylvania has about 400 open county positions (https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-cuts-work-requirements-state-staff-shortages/). Caveat: the tier percentages and FY start dates come from the article and my recollection of the law and should be re-verified.
first_30_days: Target North Carolina, where about 100 counties buy independently in small increments. Recruit 2 retired state QC reviewers as advisers. Offer 3 county DSS directors a free retrospective audit of 100 closed cases, showing errors the county's own review missed. Convert to a paid pilot under the county's small-purchase threshold. Confirm security requirements (in-tenant deployment, redaction) before touching real case files.

title: Scam-Baiting AI Fleet Selling Mule Intel
one_liner: Thousands of realistic AI victims answer scammers' calls and chats around the clock, extract the accounts and wallets they are told to pay, and hand them to the holding institutions before real victims do.
customer: Banks, neobanks, BaaS sponsor banks, stablecoin issuers, exchanges and payment apps. Telcos are a secondary buyer.
problem: Scam cash-out depends on mule accounts and wallets, but institutions learn about them only after victims pay. Scam revenue reached about $17B in 2025, and AI-enabled operations earn far more per operation, while defense stays manual and reactive.
solution: Persona-driven voice and messaging agents on real-time speech-to-speech models answer phone numbers seeded onto scam lead lists and respond to smishing and wrong-number openers. They keep scammers engaged (burning their labor), record payment instructions, and extract payee accounts, wallets and gift-card destinations. Evidence-graded indicators go via API to the institution that holds the account so it can freeze and close before a real victim pays.
why_now: Real-time speech models made convincing multi-turn calls cheap in 2025-26. Stablecoin issuers and cross-industry units now freeze funds quickly, and the US-UK scam-center coordination raises appetite for actionable intelligence.
revenue_model: $200-1,000 per confirmed account or wallet plus $5-20K per month subscriptions, and data licensing to fraud vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Scammers' scarce resource is human operator time, so AI victims raise their cost per victim while producing intelligence with zero victim cost. Institutions pay far more for pre-loss intelligence than for post-loss forensics.
first_30_days: Build 20 personas across phone and WhatsApp. Run them against inbound spam numbers and produce about 100 verified indicators. Sell 2 neobanks and 1 exchange a $10K paid pilot, with counsel reviewing recording-consent rules first.

title: Critical-Error Benchmark for Legal Transcription AI
one_liner: An independent, reporter-built test suite that scores transcription AI on the errors that lose cases, such as dropped negatives, swapped numbers, wrong speaker and uh-huh versus huh-uh. Court and law-firm buyers pay for procurement reports, and vendors pay for certification.
customer: State court administrative offices and county courts running digital-recording or AI pilots. Large law firm innovation and procurement teams. Insurer litigation-management groups. The AI transcription vendors themselves, who buy a certification badge.
problem: Every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy, measured as word error rate on clean audio. That metric treats 'I did not see him' becoming 'I did see him' as one wrong word in six, no worse than a dropped 'the.' Reporters know the real failure points: negations, numbers (fifteen versus fifty), proper names, speaker attribution in crosstalk, uh-huh versus huh-uh, soft-spoken witnesses, and interpreted testimony. Court procurement officers and firm buyers have no independent comparison, so RFPs copy vendor claims.
solution: Build a hidden test set from staged mock depositions and hearings. Working reporters play scripted witnesses and attorneys, recorded in courtroom reverb, on Zoom, with masks, accents and interpreters. Each recording has certified steno ground truth and annotated critical-error spans. Publish a Critical Error Rate per hour with per-category scores. Release a free public subset and leaderboard for credibility. Charge for private bake-offs on a buyer's own audio, graded by reporters. Sell annual certification with re-testing whenever a vendor updates its model.
why_now: Shortages are pushing courts to adopt digital and AI reporting, and Texas, North Dakota and California have all moved on it in different ways. The federal proposal for new Rule 707 signals that courts want reliability standards for machine output. Vendors are consolidating (Verbit owns Veritext). State court technology offices are writing RFPs now with no independent yardstick.
revenue_model: $15,000-$40,000 per court or firm procurement evaluation. $25,000-$75,000 per year per vendor for certification and re-testing. $3,000-$8,000 per year for benchmark subscription reports to firms and insurers. Licensing test sets to vendors under strict separation from the certification arm.
non_obvious_insight: Accuracy is measured by the people selling it. The profession that produces legal ground truth for a living is the natural auditor. A dropped 'not' is the error class that ends careers in this field, and word error rate hides it as noise.
first_30_days: Hire 8 working reporters at $75-$100 per hour for weekend sessions. Produce 20 hours of staged audio and run 6 vendors. Publish a free 'Negation Error Report' that reporter associations will share. Email 15 state court technology officers and the National Center for State Courts. Offer each vendor a free re-test to start certification conversations.

title: Vet-Verified Escrow for Puppy Purchases
one_liner: Buyer funds sit in escrow and release to the seller only after a licensed vet exam confirms the animal is healthy and the microchip matches.
customer: First-time online puppy and kitten buyers (mostly Gen Z and millennials), plus ethical breeders, rescues and rehoming sellers who lose sales to scammers. Partner clinics are the fulfillment side and insurers are the third payer.
problem: Pet-purchase scams are a top online-fraud category inside the FTC's record $15.9B of 2025 scam losses. Deposits go by Zelle, Cash App or gift card and are irreversible. Legitimate breeders cannot prove trustworthiness. Sick puppies (parvo and congenital problems) show up days after a sale, and a vet shortage means new-patient slots are scarce, so buyers skip the check.
solution: The buyer pays via card or ACH into escrow. Release requires a 72-hour exam at a partner clinic confirming health, microchip and vaccination records; failure means refund minus fee. Part of the escrow fee pays the clinic for the exam, so the clinic gains a new client with prepaid revenue. The exam visit also enrolls the pet in insurance while it is clean of pre-existing conditions, for an acquisition fee. Extensions: lost-pet reward escrow released on a microchip scan, and stud and rehoming fees.
why_now: Record scam losses and irreversible peer-to-peer payments make buyers and platforms desperate for protection. Only 48.2% of practices proactively recommend insurance, so insurers need better first-year distribution. Clinics are capacity-constrained and want reliable new patients. Delayed-payout marketplace payment APIs make escrow cheap to build.
revenue_model: 4-5% escrow fee, $40-60 insurer acquisition fee per enrolled pet, and clinic exam fees funded from the escrow. Sellers can pay for a verified-breeder badge.
non_obvious_insight: The vet exam is the only trusted, licensed, in-person oracle in the pet-purchase chain, so use it as the escrow release condition. Because the fee funds the visit, the clinic gets a paid new client, which turns the vet shortage into a pull instead of a friction.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 ethical breeders or rescues and 5 clinics in one metro. Build on Stripe Connect delayed payouts. Market to breed groups on Facebook and puppy-advice communities, and offer the first 50 transactions at a discount for testimonials.

title: Deepfake Shields for Mayors, Sold Through Risk Pools
one_liner: Long-tail likeness and voice protection for roughly 500,000 local elected officials, clerks and first responders who have no agency to police impersonation, sold as a loss-control service through municipal insurance risk pools and county election offices.
customer: State and regional municipal risk pools and cyber pools ($300-1,500 per member per year), county election offices ($500-2,000 each), and sheriffs' and police chiefs' associations.
problem: YouTube's likeness detection reached celebrities through CAA, UTA and WME in April 2026 with no path for anyone else, and voice clones need only seconds of audio (prior knowledge). Local officials are high-impact targets: a cloned 'mayor' telling finance staff to wire funds, fake curfew or polling-place notices, fake council videos. Local IT is thin (Dallas County is cutting 31 IT staff), federal election-security help to localities was scaled back in 2025 (prior knowledge), and the midterms are Nov 3, 2026.
solution: Enroll officials with consented voice and face references and monitor major platforms using existing detection APIs. Run a human takedown desk using platform impersonation policies and state deepfake statutes. Give finance staff call-back code-word protocols and quarterly voice-clone drills, and deliver evidence packs for insurers and police.
why_now: Midterm urgency, celebrity-only platform tools, and cheap high-quality voice cloning all arrive together. Pools face rising social-engineering claims (inference), and EU Article 50 plus platform enforcement raise expectations that impersonations get pulled quickly.
revenue_model: A per-member fee paid by the pool, per-incident takedown fees, drill fees, and premium credits negotiated with the pool.
non_obvious_insight: The 'agency' that long-tail people lack is the insurance pool. It already pays social-engineering claims, has member-services budgets, and can buy for a thousand towns in one sale. Framing the product as claims reduction rather than reputation management is what unlocks the budget.
first_30_days: Interview 5 pool loss-control managers and sell a $499 election-season kit to 20 county clerks. Run a free voice-clone drill for one pool's treasurers association to produce a claim-reduction case study.

title: Baseline: Bank-Feed Proof of Displacement Costs
one_liner: An app that reconstructs a displaced family's 'normal' spending from pre-loss bank statements and computes the exact increase that Additional Living Expense coverage owes, in carrier-ready format.
customer: Public adjusters and disaster-recovery nonprofits (paying per file), and carriers or TPAs handling long-tail displaced-household claims (paying per active ALE file per month). Consumers use it free.
problem: ALE pays the increase over normal living costs, not the total, so proving it requires a baseline that almost no family has. Adjusters spend hours rebuilding it from memory and shoeboxes, families under-claim (groceries, laundry, mileage, pet boarding, storage, higher utilities) or document sloppily, and disputes turn ugly. With California's new smoke-damage law (AB 1795, effective Jan 1, 2027) barring insurers from cutting off ALE until the home is restored, thousands of standing-home households will run ALE claims for years with heavy documentation demands.
solution: A privacy-first tool that ingests 12 months of pre-loss bank or card data (via open-banking link or uploaded statements), builds a per-category baseline, then diffs it month by month against post-loss spending, matches receipts, and flags gaps the family can legitimately claim (extra mileage, meal delta, rented furniture, storage). Output is an ALE ledger with audit trail in the format desk adjusters actually accept, plus a deadline tracker for policy ALE time limits. Processing is on-device or in a private enclave, and the data is deleted after export.
why_now: More than 13,000 standing-home smoke claims from the Eaton and Palisades fires are still unresolved 20 months later, a lawsuit accuses Farmers' vendor of substandard assessments, and AB 1795 makes ALE duration a live issue. LLM parsing of messy statements and receipts is now cheap and accurate enough to be a product. Carriers are cutting adjusters (entry-level postings down about 50% since 2025) but ALE files still need documentation, so automation that delivers clean files is welcomed.
revenue_model: Public adjusters and recovery groups pay $99-$199 per file. Carriers and TPAs pay $30-$60 per active ALE file per month, or $75-$150 per closed file, in exchange for fewer touches and fewer complaints. Optional referral fees from moving, storage and rental-furniture vendors for legitimate, claimable purchases.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the industry records 'normal.' The claim's central number, the increase over normal, is unmeasured on the policyholder's side, and adjusters know most under-claiming is not a coverage denial but the family's inability to prove what they used to spend. Bank data is the only pre-loss record the insured always has.
first_30_days: Build a prototype that categorizes statement CSVs and PDFs into ALE categories and produces a monthly delta ledger. Offer it free to 10 Altadena and Palisades public adjusters and to two survivor-support networks in exchange for feedback and 20 anonymized-consent pilot files. Ask two carrier ALE desk managers to review the output format and sign a paid pilot at $50 per file for 200 files. Prepare a privacy policy and data-deletion promise, because trust is the product.
